Hey Jared — happy to jump in. Short answers + examples below; we can expand on the call.

1) SDK & auth - Recommended: service-account + short-lived tokens. For Dedicated/Private we offer a service account flow where you mint short-lived tokens via a signed JWT (your KMS/HSM signs) against our token exchange endpoint. We support key rotation; examples in the quickstart (see attached schema-snippet.json with Node example). For Hub: you can also integrate our KMS connectors.

2) Chat vs Completions for structured output - For strongly structured payloads and tool-calling, our chat API with function/tool calling is the recommended path. Benefits: explicit schema for arguments, first-class tool invocation lifecycle, and deterministic JSON in many cases. If you need hyper-strict schema validation, you can combine chat + function definition and also run a final schema validator on the JSON. Completions can work but require more prompt engineering and brittle parsing.

Example (chat + function):
- messages: [{role: "system", content: "You are an assistant that outputs JSON matching the action schema."}, {role: "user", content: "Create a ticket for login error"}]
- functions: [{name: "create_ticket", parameters: {type: "object", properties: {action_type: {type: "string"}, target_id: {type: "string"}, confidence: {type: "number"}, metadata: {type: "object"}}}}]

3) Tokenization & max_tokens - Our runtime enforces a total token limit per request (prompt + response). For a 2000-token context and expected ~300-token output, set max_tokens to 400 to provide headroom; the server will truncate prompt-side overflows per your policy (you can choose to reject requests instead). Cost is per input+output token.

Stop tokens & streaming: streaming sends incremental tokens as they are generated; the stream ends when generation finishes or the model emits a stop sequence. If you configure stop tokens, the generator will stop production once the tokenized stop is produced — that will trigger stream end. For function/tool calling we stream the 'arguments' field progressively; the final chunk includes the complete JSON.

4) Embeddings & reranker - Batch embeddings for throughput — send batches sized to fit your memory (we recommend 128-512 depending on model dims and your host RAM). We return a list of embeddings in the same order. Rerankers — typical pattern: coarse retrieval via embeddings (top-N), then rerank via model or a learned model. Watch out for truncation on long docs; keep canonical text snippets for embedding.
